Where does esports prize money actually go?

Overview

What this project does

The analysis combines public Kaggle esports datasets with geographic reference data to examine how prize money is distributed across titles, genres and continents — and whether that distribution follows any predictable pattern.

Two Python notebooks carry out the end-to-end work: Esport_test.ipynb handles data ingestion, cleaning and exploratory charting, and earnings by games and genre.ipynb runs the statistical distribution and correlation analysis. The findings then feed a Dash/Plotly web dashboard that lets anyone filter the results themselves.

Technical detail · Notebook 1

Esport_test.ipynb — building the pipeline

Before any chart can be trusted, the underlying data has to be ingested, joined and typed correctly. This notebook does that work and runs the first exploratory pass.

Data ingestion

Three tables were pulled directly into Pandas using the kagglehub API against the jackodavid/esports-earnings-for-players-teams-by-game dataset:

  • Player earnings — 1,000 rows × 8 columns (player, handle, country, game, genre, total prize)
  • Team earnings — 928 rows × 6 columns (team, total prize, tournaments, game, genre)
  • Country / continent codes — 262 rows × 4 columns, used to enrich players with region

  1. Standardize join keys

    Country codes were upper-cased and stripped of whitespace on both sides before joining, since inconsistent casing silently breaks merges.

  2. Left-join geography onto players

    Player records were merged against the country/continent table on the two-letter country code, adding Continent_Name and Country_Name to every player.

  3. Map games to release dates

    A manual lookup dictionary (e.g. CS:GO → 2012-08-21, Fortnite → 2017-07-21) was applied and converted to real datetime64 values, enabling the later release-year analysis.

  4. Fix identifier types

    PlayerId and TeamId were cast from numeric to string, preventing pandas from accidentally summing or averaging what are really labels, not quantities.

  5. Validate

    Null counts and duplicate checks confirmed a clean dataset (0 duplicate rows) before moving to analysis — aside from a handful of unmapped continent codes.

Technical detail · Notebook 2

earnings by games and genre.ipynb — the statistics

This notebook works from the 690-game reference file to ask three questions: how concentrated is prize money, which genres actually earn it, and what correlates with a game's total earnings.

Prize concentration follows a Pareto pattern

Games were sorted by total earnings and split into rank groups of 10. Plotting each group's earnings on a log scale reveals a near-linear decay — the signature of a power-law, winner-take-most distribution.

Genre economics: total vs. average

Ranking genres by total earnings tells a different story than ranking them by average earnings per title — the two views highlight different competitive dynamics.

What correlates with earnings?

A Pearson correlation was computed across each game's player count, tournament count and total earnings.

Metric pairrStrength
Players vs. Earnings0.72Strong
Players vs. Tournaments0.79Strong
Tournaments vs. Earnings0.53Moderate
Correlation isn't causation, and the notebook is careful to frame each result as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion:
Players ↔ Earnings (0.72): a larger player base could drive publisher investment in prize pools — or high prize pools could be what attracts players in the first place.
Tournaments ↔ Earnings (0.53, weakest link): earnings look concentrated in a few "Tier 1" mega-events rather than spread evenly across every hosted tournament.
Synthesis

Three takeaways

Earnings are winner-take-most

A small group of flagship titles captures the large majority of global prize money, and the drop-off to the long tail is exponential, not gradual.

Genre shapes the business model

MOBA wins on scale (fewer, larger events); Battle Royale wins on density (high earnings per title); high title-count genres like Fighting Games stay niche financially.

Player base is the strongest signal

Of the three metrics tested, a game's active player and tournament counts track earnings more closely than tournament count alone — grassroots scale seems to matter more than event frequency.

The finished product

An interactive dashboard, built on these findings

The last step turns the analysis into something a non-technical stakeholder can explore directly: a Dash/Plotly web app with live filters, KPI cards and drill-down charts covering the $411M, 1,032-player flagship dataset.

01 · Overview & Objective

Turn player-level earnings data into a decision-ready story.

  • Compare prize money across games and genres
  • Understand how earnings are distributed geographically
  • Identify top players and test what correlates with a game's earnings
  • Package the findings into a filterable, interactive dashboard
02 · Data & Tools

Two datasets, one pipeline.

  • Flagship dataset (KaggleHub API): 1,032 players, 928 teams, 10 major titles, 56 countries — powers the dashboard
  • Genre reference dataset: 690 games across 12 genres — powers the distribution and correlation analysis
  • Stack: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Seaborn/Matplotlib, Plotly, Scikit-learn, Dash
03 · Notebook 1 — Data Pipeline

Ingest, clean, and validate before analyzing.

  • Pulled player/team/country data via the KaggleHub API
  • Standardized and joined country codes to add continent & country
  • Mapped each game to its release date; fixed ID columns to strings
  • Verified zero duplicates before moving to analysis
04 · Notebook 2 — Prize Concentration

Earnings follow a Pareto distribution.

  • Games ranked and grouped into buckets of 10 by total earnings
  • Log-scale plot shows near-linear decay — a classic power law
  • Top 10 games alone earned over $1B in this reference dataset
04 · Notebook 2 — Prize Concentration

The top 20% of rank groups hold 90%+ of earnings.

  • Cumulative earnings curve flattens almost immediately
  • Confirms a small set of flagship titles drives the whole economy
  • The long tail of 500+ games contributes only marginal earnings
05 · Notebook 2 — Genre Economics

MOBA wins on scale. Battle Royale wins on density.

  • MOBA leads total earnings — few events, very high stakes
  • Battle Royale leads average earnings per title
  • Fighting Games have the most titles but the smallest prize pools
06 · Notebook 2 — Correlation

Player base tracks earnings more than event count does.

  • Players ↔ Earnings: r = 0.72 (strong)
  • Players ↔ Tournaments: r = 0.79 (strong)
  • Tournaments ↔ Earnings: r = 0.53 (moderate — prize pools concentrate in a few mega-events)
